hero.title: Earth is dancing. NISAR can see the steps.
hero.subtitle: NISAR, the new NASA-ISRO radar satellite, scans nearly all of Earth's land every 12 days, through clouds and darkness. Every kind of change, a forest cut, a field planted, a flood, leaves its own signature in its two radar channels. Here is how to read them.

channels.title: Two ways of listening
text: NISAR sends down microwave pulses 24 centimeters long and listens to the echoes in two ways.
HH hears echoes that come back the way they left: smooth ground, and pulses that bounce between water and a trunk or a wall.
HV hears echoes twisted by bouncing around inside leaves and branches. It measures living canopy.

Give every hectare a spot by its two echoes and each kind of surface finds its own place: water at the bottom left, forests at the top right, cities and flooded trees far right. Decibels (dB) are the radar's loudness scale: +3 dB is twice as loud.

chips.label: Open water
chips.text: Calm water reflects the pulse away like a mirror: almost no echo in either channel.

chips.label: Bare field
chips.text: Bare soil sends back a modest HH echo and very little HV: there is nothing to twist the pulse.

chips.label: Full-grown crop
chips.text: The same fields in September: leaves and stalks scatter the pulse, and HV is 10 dB louder than in May.

chips.label: Forest
chips.text: A forest canopy scatters the pulse in every direction, so HV is strong and steady.

chips.label: City
chips.text: Walls and streets bounce the pulse straight back to the satellite: the loudest HH of all.

examples.title: A crop growing: wheat
examples.text: In winter, Punjab's fields grow wheat. As the plants fill in, their leaves twist the radar pulse: across 70,752 cultivated hectares, the median HV climbed 3.3 dB between November and February. The April harvest takes it back down to bare soil.

examples.kicker: Punjab, India (the same fields, the same year)
examples.title: Rice standing in water
examples.text: In the monsoon the same fields are flooded and planted with rice. Now the pulse bounces off the water, up the stalks and straight back: the median HH jumped 6.9 dB between mid-July and mid-September while HV rose only 4.1 dB. The gap between the channels widened from 9 to 12 dB. Two crops, two radar channels.

examples.title: A flood hidden under trees
examples.text: Tropical Storm Edouard flooded East Texas forests in early September 2026. From above, the canopy hides the water. NISAR's 24 cm waves reach the ground: on the pass during the storm, 3,572 forested hectares jumped 3 dB or more in HH while HV held still, the double bounce off water and trunks. Twelve days later the water had drained.

examples.title: A forest cut down
examples.text: Rondonia is one of the most deforested states in the Amazon, and clearing happens in the dry season. When the canopy goes, so does its scattering: the hectares cleared in this window lost about 8 dB of HV. In this 6 km window the dark new clearings appear between June and October; across the whole 40 km box, 1,801 forested hectares lost 3 dB or more of HV.

examples.title: An ice sheet's summer
examples.text: Over ice, NISAR listens with HH alone. Wet snow absorbs the pulse; as summer goes on, rough bare ice and refrozen crust send more of it back. In the window shown, HH rose about 7 dB by the August 19 pass and settled again by October; across the whole melt zone in this box the rise was 4 to 5 dB.

proof.title: Does it work?
proof.intro: We taught a model the signatures using 170 US places where other sources already say what happened: NASA's optical forest-loss alerts, wildfire perimeters, water maps and cropland maps. Then we tested it on 72 places in 12 states it had never seen.

items.baseline_label: found by picking land at random
items.statement: It finds forest loss. Pointing at just 1.7% of the land, it found 54 of every 100 hectares of real forest loss. Picking the same amount of land at random would find about 2.
items.detail: 1,822 hectares of reference forest loss in the 12 unseen states.

items.statement: It recognizes growing crops. When it says a field is growing a crop, it is right 63 times in 100; a guess would be right about 10 times.
items.detail: Checked against the USDA Cropland Data Layer.

items.statement: When SARstellar says a hectare changed, it really did 66 times in 100, against 19 by guessing.
items.detail: Any labeled change: forest loss, fire, open-water flood or crop growth.

items.statement: Forest loss lives in HV. Listening to HV alone, the model finds it 6 times better than listening to HH alone: the canopy echo is what disappears.
items.detail: Same model retrained with one channel at a time; ranking quality on the unseen states.

items.statement: NISAR beats the radar we had before. At the same detection rate, 31 of every 100 NISAR forest-loss alerts were real, against 4 of 100 for Sentinel-1, Europe's shorter-wavelength radar: 7.8 times more often right.
items.detail: 37 forest-loss sites, same hectares, same reference (SARstellar v1 benchmark).

items.statement: It travels. Trained only on US places, it still found 54% of the forest loss NASA's optical satellites recorded in Rondonia, Brazil, while pointing at 1.3% of the land.

limits: Open-water floods were hard to tell apart from two passes alone at our test sites, and grass fires barely register at L-band. We show those, not hide them.
The reference maps are imperfect: optical satellites miss cloudy weeks and fire perimeters include unburned patches.
Floods under trees and ice changes have no labeled test set yet; we show them as physics, measured but not scored.
Test places were chosen where changes happened, so these numbers describe those places, not how common change is everywhere.
NISAR's 2026 data are provisional releases; NASA may reprocess them.

applications.title: Deforestation through the clouds
applications.text: The tropics are cloudy for months. Radar alerts don't wait for a clear day.

applications.title: Floods under forests
applications.text: Map where water spreads beneath the canopy, where optical satellites see only trees.

applications.title: Rice and food security
applications.text: Track when Asia's paddies are flooded and planted, every 12 days.

applications.title: Crop calendars everywhere
applications.text: Planting, growth and harvest for any field on Earth, cloud or no cloud.

applications.title: Ice in a warming world
applications.text: Follow the melt season across Greenland and Antarctica, pass by pass.
